L213: In-frame deletion mutants of E. coli EC1250 were constructed as described by Link et al. (【69†10】) with some modifications.E. coli EC1250 was first transformed with a pKO3 derivative by using heat shock or electroporation (【65†1】). Transformants were selected at 30°C on LB plates containing chloramphenicol. On the second day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended in 0.5 ml of LB medium and diluted 10^{2}-, 10^{3}-, and 10^{4}-fold.
L214: A portion (300 to 500 μl) of each dilution was plated onto prewarmed LB-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 43°C overnight. On the third day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended and diluted as described above, plated on LB-sucrose plates, and incubated at 30°C overnight. On the fourth day, 100 to 500 colonies from the LB-sucrose plates were picked on LB-sucrose and LB-sucrose-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 30°C overnight.
L215: When possible, an additional screening on sulfur-free M63 minimal medium plates was done to find out which of the positive colonies (sucrose resistant and chloramphenicol sensitive) were unable to grow with taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source and thus were likely to carry the desired deletion. Putative deletion mutants were analyzed using colony PCR withTaq DNA polymerase.
L216: A single colony was resuspended into 20 μl of sterile deionized water, from which 1 μl was added to a 50-μl PCR mixture (【65†1】). The sequence of interest was amplified using the external primers used for the construction of the deletion; PCR products were analyzed on 0.8% TAE-agarose gels. Positive clones were purified on LB plates at least three times, checking each time for the presence of the desired in-frame deletion by colony PCR.
L217: For the construction of multiple EC1250 deletion mutants, a deletion mutant was subjected to another round of deletion as described above. Overall, the frequency of in-frame deletions obtained in successful experiments amounted to 1.4% of the putatively positive clones that were screened.
L218: ### Construction of tauD and ssuD tauDmutants.
L219: Since efforts to obtain an in-frame deletion oftauD remained unsuccessful, a tauD mutant ofE. coli EC1250 was constructed by P1 transduction (【77†11】). The tauD::lacZ fusion of the E. coli MC4100 derivative MW108 [Φ(tauD::lacZ)(λplacMu9)] (【57†21】) was transduced into E. coli EC1250.
L220: Kanamycin-resistant transductants were screened for inability to grow on M63 minimal medium with taurine as a sulfur source and for the formation of blue colonies on M63 minimal medium supplemented with glutathione as a sulfur source and X-Gal to confirm the presence of thelacZ fusion. To obtain an ssuD tauD double mutant, an EC1250 mutant with ssuD deleted was used as a recipient.
L221: ### Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants.
L222: Restriction sites which are unique within the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons were used to construct the plasmids shown in Fig. 【68†1】 and listed in Table 【70†2】. Plasmids for the complementation analysis of tau deletions were constructed in pUC19 (【75†26】), starting from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】). Plasmids required for the complementation analysis of ssudeletions were constructed in pBluescript II KS, starting with plasmid pME4221, which carries the entire ssu operon on a 5.6-kbEcoRI fragment (【59†24】).
L223: Growth of deletion mutants transformed with the appropriate plasmid was measured in 5 ml of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with taurine or butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Cultures were incubated at 37°C overnight, and the optical density at 600 nm was recorded on the following day.
L224: Alternatively, when growth of strains was investigated over a longer period of time, single colonies of the deletion mutant as well as of the strain transformed with the appropriate plasmid were resuspended in 50 μl of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, from which 20 μl was spotted on an M63 minimal medium plate containing taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source. Sulfur-limited solid media were prepared by the addition of 1.5 to 2% SeaPlaque agarose (FMC BioProducts).

L228: ### Construction of in-frame deletions in the tau andssu operons.
L229: Figure 【78†2】shows the functional transport components in deletion mutants that were constructed to probe for the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonate compounds. A first group of mutants lacked one of the putative periplasmic binding proteins (Fig.【78†2】A and B) or the membrane-associated components TauBC or SsuCB (Fig. 【78†2】D and E). A second group included constructs that were defective in the corresponding components of both transport systems at the same time.
L230: A mutant devoid of both periplasmic binding proteins (Fig. 【78†2】C) allowed exploration of whether or not certain alkanesulfonates can enter the cell in the absence of the periplasmic components. Similarly, a mutant lacking the membrane-associated components of both systems (Fig. 【78†2】F) was expected to be defective in the uptake of all sulfonate sulfur sources transported via the TauABC and SsuABC systems.
L231: A third group of mutants carried various combinations of deletions that abolished the function of a periplasmic component, an integral membrane component, and an ATP-binding protein of either transport system. Six out of the eight possible combinations of multiple deletion mutants were obtained (Fig. 【78†2】G to L), and the growth properties of these mutants were expected to provide information on the exchangeability of components between the TauABC and SsuABC transport systems.
L232: Attempts to obtain the multiple deletion ΔtauABC and ΔssuA ΔssuB ΔtauC strains by using the chromosomal mutagenesis system described by Link et al. (【69†10】) were unsuccessful, and their construction was not pursued further.

L236: In addition to mutants with components of the TauABC and SsuABC transport systems deleted, strains lacking either the SsuD or TauD desulfonation enzyme were constructed. These mutants served to correlate growth with a particular alkanesulfonate as a sulfur source with the presence of either one of these enzymes and to verify whether the range of alkanesulfonates utilized corresponded to the previously established substrate range of the purified enzymes (【58†3】, 【60†4】).
L237: An ssuD tauD double mutant was important for establishing the amount of background growth in growth experiments. Since this strain lacked both α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase and alkanesulfonate monooxygenase, growth of this mutant on medium containing a particular alkanesulfonate as the only sulfur source was considered to be due to nonsulfonate sulfur contaminants present in the alkanesulfonate preparation used.
L238: ### Growth of wild-type and deletion strains with alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources.
L239: Growth was tested in a medium containing one of the following sulfonates as the only sulfur source: taurine, isethionate (2-hydroxyethanesulfonic acid), 3-aminopropanesulfonate, HEPES, MOPS, PIPES, 2-(4-pyridyl)ethanesulfonate,N-phenyltaurine, 1,3-dioxo-2-isoindoline-ethanesulfonate, 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonate, sulfoacetate, ethanesulfonate, propanesulfonate, butanesulfonate, pentanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate, octanesulfonate, decanesulfonate, and dodecanesulfonate.
L240: All of these compounds have been shown to be substrates for the TauD and/or the SsuD enzyme (【58†3】, 【60†4】). The qualitative assessment of growth with each of the 19 sulfonates tested was based on a comparison of the growth characteristics of each mutant with growth of the wild type. The wild type defined the upper level of growth, while the ssuD tauD double mutant served as a reference for zero growth with a particular sulfonate sulfur source.
L241: Growth of the deletion mutants on different sulfur sources was graded as described in Table 【80†3】, footnotea. The growth curves of the ΔssuA and the ΔssuCB mutants shown in Fig.【81†3】 illustrate the four arbitrarily established growth categories. From Fig. 【81†3】 it is also evident that growth with sulfonate sulfur sources was diauxic, with a first, minor growth phase presumably supported by contaminating sulfate and a second, longer growth phase reflecting sulfonate utilization.
L242: Diauxic growth was not observed when strains were cultured with sulfate as a source of sulfur. Furthermore, mutants in which transporter genes were deleted grew faster than the wild-type strain on either sulfate or sulfonates as a sulfur source. However, depending on the sulfonate sulfur source tested, fluctuations in the growth rate and length of the lag phase were noted.
L243: Since strains lacking TauD or SsuD grew like the wild type, we presume that these phenomena have their origin at the level of the transport of alkanesulfonates.

L248: Table【80†3】 summarizes the growth phenotypes of the different E. coli constructs that carried one or more deletions in the genes for the putative TauABC and SsuABC transporters. L284: As is evident from Table 【80†3】, propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate served as sulfur sources and enabled some growth of all deletion mutants examined. This suggests that these compounds enter the cell to some extent by a mechanism different from active transport by the SsuABC and TauABC systems.
L285: To test whether triple deletion mutants such as strains EC1250 ΔtauA ΔssuB ΔtauC, EC1250 ΔssuA ΔtauB ΔssuC, EC1250 ΔssuA ΔtauBC, and EC1250 ΔtauAΔssuCB are able to form functional hybrid transporters, these strains were inoculated into minimal medium containing one of the alkanesulfonates that are transported by both the SsuABC and the TauABC systems. The absence of growth under these conditions indicated that productive interaction between components of the two transport systems does not occur.
L286: ### Complementation analysis of deletion mutants.
L287: For the construction of complementation plasmids, it was assumed that chromosomal in-frame deletions would not affect the expression of the genes located upstream of the deleted gene or group of genes. Therefore, the genetic information available on the complementation plasmids started with the regulatory sequences of the operon of interest and ended with the sequence of the gene that had been deleted on the chromosome (Fig. 【68†1】).
L288: In the case of mutants with multiple deletions, the complementation of each deletion was investigated separately, if necessary in an intermediary deletion mutant.
L289: ssu deletion mutants carrying the appropriatessu complementation plasmid showed wild-type growth. However, tauA and tauB deletion mutants carrying the corresponding complementation plasmids pME4727 and pME4726 did not grow on taurine to the wild-type level. This effect was traced to the presence of the tauA gene or 540 bp of its proximal part on the high-copy-number plasmid pUC19 (data not shown).
L290: The reason for the severe growth inhibition exerted by these plasmids is not known, but complementation of tauA andtauB deletions with constructs based on the low-copy-number vector pET-24a(+) (pME4733, pME4734) was successful.
L291: To confirm that an in-frame deletion of tauA did not affect expression of tauD, α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase activity was measured as described previously (【58†3】) in cell extracts of E. coli EC1250 and EC1250 ΔtauA grown on butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Identical levels of TauD specific activity were obtained from both wild-type EC1250 and mutant cells lacking TauA. The tauAdeletion thus did not influence the expression of the downstream genes.
L292: Taken together, these results show that the chromosomally located in-frame deletions did not affect other gene functions and that the observed growth phenotypes were solely due to the deletion of the gene of interest.
L293: ## DISCUSSION
L294: The E. coli TauABCD and SsuEADCB systems for the assimilation of sulfur from taurine and other alkanesulfonates have previously been characterized at the level of the biochemistry of desulfonation (【58†3】, 【60†4】). Besides containing the structural genes directly involved in desulfonation, the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons are thought to encode components of ABC transporters for sulfonates (【57†21】, 【59†24】).
L295: Based on the results from growth experiments and on sequence data, we postulate that TauABC and SsuABC form two distinct ABC transporters for uptake of alkanesulfonates. Sequence comparisons indicate that ABC-type transport systems involved in microbial desulfonation are also present inBacillus subtilis (【86†23】) and Pseudomonas putida (【87†25】). Like in E. coli, these are encoded in the same transcription unit as the desulfonating enzyme. The deletion analysis of the E.
L296: coli taurine and alkanesulfonate transport systems presented here goes beyond amino acid sequence comparisons; it attempts to characterize these systems in terms of the substrate range and functional exchangeability of their components.
L297: Our results demonstrate that the TauABC and the SsuABC systems complement each other with respect to the range of substrates transported. The substrate ranges of TauD and SsuD were to a large extent reflected in the substrate range of the corresponding ABC transporter. The substrate range of the SsuABC transporter fit that of the SsuD alkanesulfonate monooxygenase.
L298: This correlation is not maintained for the TauABC transport system, which was unable to transport HEPES, MOPS, and propanesulfonate, although these compounds are substrates for the TauD enzyme (【58†3】). Thus, two systems for alkanesulfonate uptake and metabolism are available in E. coli, with TauABCD being specifically involved in uptake and desulfonation of taurine and SsuEADCB being an uptake and desulfonation system for a wide range of alkanesulfonates other than taurine.
L299: In the systems examined in this work, deletion strains that produced the substrate-binding protein of one transporter and the membrane component of the other did not grow with the sulfonates transported by either TauABC or SsuABC. Also, the formation of productive hybrid transporters in which the membrane component would be composed of the ATP-binding protein (SsuB or TauB) of one transporter and the membrane-spanning protein (SsuC or TauC) of the other transporter did not occur.
L300: The failure of hybrid transporters to support growth extended to alkanesulfonates that were common substrates of both wild-type transporters. It therefore appears to be due to the lack of interaction between the individual components of hybrid systems rather than to restrictions imposed by substrate specificity. An exception was noted when propanesulfonate or butanesulfonate was offered as a sulfur source.
L301: These compounds enabled growth, at respectable levels, of strains EC1250 ΔtauA ΔssuA and EC1250 ΔtauBC ΔssuCB as well as of mutants producing hybrid transporters (Table 【80†3】). In addition to being transported by the TauABC and/or the SsuABC system, propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate appear to enter the cell by an as-yet-unknown mechanism. Since both compounds are fully ionized under physiological conditions (【88†8】), their entrance into the cytoplasm by passive diffusion seems unlikely.
L302: There are few reports on functional exchangeability of the components of ABC transporters in the literature. ATP-binding proteins of ABC transporters have domains in common that were shown to be functionally interchangeable in the recombinant hybrid protein HisP-MalK ofSalmonella typhimurium. This protein was fully active in maltose transport but failed to complement a hisP deletion mutation (【89†17】).
L303: This observation indicated that HisP and MalK share domains that are exchangeable, whereas other domains confer system specificity by providing for interactions between the membrane-spanning protein and the ATP-binding protein (【90†12】, 【89†17】). Furthermore, complete ATP-binding proteins have successfully been exchanged between the Mal and Ugp transporters, which in E. coli transport maltose and sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, respectively (【91†5】).
L304: The N-terminal parts of the UgpC and MalK proteins exhibit approximately 60% sequence identity, which is much higher than the 35.6% sequence identity over the first 150 amino acids between the TauB and SsuB proteins.
L305: Periplasmic binding proteins for sulfonates and sulfate esters fromE. coli, B. subtilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and P. putida share between 22 and 45% sequence identity (【87†25】). They are less than 15% identical to other solute-binding proteins and form a family of binding proteins separate from those previously defined by Tam and Saier (【92†19】).
L306: TauA and SsuA are members of this family, but they exhibit only 22.7% sequence identity and were found to be unable to substitute for each other (Table 【80†3】). This is in contrast to theE. coli uptake systems for sulfate and thiosulfate (【93†18】) and lysine-arginine-ornithine and histidine (【94†13】), where two binding proteins of overlapping substrate specificity interact with a unique membrane component.
L307: The sulfate- and thiosulfate-binding proteins show 45% sequence identity, and the lysine-arginine-ornithine- and histidine-binding proteins are 70% identical.
L308: The proteins of the two postulated independent transport systems ofE. coli for taurine on the one hand and alkanesulfonates on the other exhibit low sequence identity but share a common physiological role. As documented by the mechanisms regulating gene expression in these systems, they both are involved in scavenging sulfur for growth.

L213: In-frame deletion mutants of E. coli EC1250 were constructed as described by Link et al. (【69†10】) with some modifications.E. coli EC1250 was first transformed with a pKO3 derivative by using heat shock or electroporation (【65†1】). Transformants were selected at 30°C on LB plates containing chloramphenicol. On the second day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended in 0.5 ml of LB medium and diluted 10^{2}-, 10^{3}-, and 10^{4}-fold.
L214: A portion (300 to 500 μl) of each dilution was plated onto prewarmed LB-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 43°C overnight. On the third day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended and diluted as described above, plated on LB-sucrose plates, and incubated at 30°C overnight. On the fourth day, 100 to 500 colonies from the LB-sucrose plates were picked on LB-sucrose and LB-sucrose-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 30°C overnight.
L215: When possible, an additional screening on sulfur-free M63 minimal medium plates was done to find out which of the positive colonies (sucrose resistant and chloramphenicol sensitive) were unable to grow with taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source and thus were likely to carry the desired deletion. Putative deletion mutants were analyzed using colony PCR withTaq DNA polymerase.
L216: A single colony was resuspended into 20 μl of sterile deionized water, from which 1 μl was added to a 50-μl PCR mixture (【65†1】). The sequence of interest was amplified using the external primers used for the construction of the deletion; PCR products were analyzed on 0.8% TAE-agarose gels. Positive clones were purified on LB plates at least three times, checking each time for the presence of the desired in-frame deletion by colony PCR.
L217: For the construction of multiple EC1250 deletion mutants, a deletion mutant was subjected to another round of deletion as described above. Overall, the frequency of in-frame deletions obtained in successful experiments amounted to 1.4% of the putatively positive clones that were screened.
L218: ### Construction of tauD and ssuD tauDmutants.
L219: Since efforts to obtain an in-frame deletion oftauD remained unsuccessful, a tauD mutant ofE. coli EC1250 was constructed by P1 transduction (【77†11】). The tauD::lacZ fusion of the E. coli MC4100 derivative MW108 [Φ(tauD::lacZ)(λplacMu9)] (【57†21】) was transduced into E. coli EC1250.
L220: Kanamycin-resistant transductants were screened for inability to grow on M63 minimal medium with taurine as a sulfur source and for the formation of blue colonies on M63 minimal medium supplemented with glutathione as a sulfur source and X-Gal to confirm the presence of thelacZ fusion. To obtain an ssuD tauD double mutant, an EC1250 mutant with ssuD deleted was used as a recipient.
L221: ### Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants.
L222: Restriction sites which are unique within the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons were used to construct the plasmids shown in Fig. 【68†1】 and listed in Table 【70†2】. Plasmids for the complementation analysis of tau deletions were constructed in pUC19 (【75†26】), starting from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】). Plasmids required for the complementation analysis of ssudeletions were constructed in pBluescript II KS, starting with plasmid pME4221, which carries the entire ssu operon on a 5.6-kbEcoRI fragment (【59†24】).
L223: Growth of deletion mutants transformed with the appropriate plasmid was measured in 5 ml of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with taurine or butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Cultures were incubated at 37°C overnight, and the optical density at 600 nm was recorded on the following day.
L224: Alternatively, when growth of strains was investigated over a longer period of time, single colonies of the deletion mutant as well as of the strain transformed with the appropriate plasmid were resuspended in 50 μl of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, from which 20 μl was spotted on an M63 minimal medium plate containing taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source. Sulfur-limited solid media were prepared by the addition of 1.5 to 2% SeaPlaque agarose (FMC BioProducts).
L225: Two plasmids that contain the ssu and tauregulatory sequences located upstream of the ssu andtau operons were constructed (【57†21】, 【59†24】). A 340-bpBamHI-EcoRI fragment from plasmid pME4204 (【59†24】) containing the ssu regulatory elements was ligated into pUC19, leading to plasmid pME4822.
L226: For the construction of plasmid pME4821, which carries the tau regulatory sequences, a 450-bp BamHI-EcoRI fragment was PCR amplified from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】) using primers JP7 and JP8 (【57†21】) and finally subcloned into pUC19.
L227: ## RESULTS
L228: ### Construction of in-frame deletions in the tau andssu operons.
L229: Figure 【78†2】shows the functional transport components in deletion mutants that were constructed to probe for the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonate compounds. A first group of mutants lacked one of the putative periplasmic binding proteins (Fig.【78†2】A and B) or the membrane-associated components TauBC or SsuCB (Fig. 【78†2】D and E). A second group included constructs that were defective in the corresponding components of both transport systems at the same time.
L230: A mutant devoid of both periplasmic binding proteins (Fig. 【78†2】C) allowed exploration of whether or not certain alkanesulfonates can enter the cell in the absence of the periplasmic components. Similarly, a mutant lacking the membrane-associated components of both systems (Fig. 【78†2】F) was expected to be defective in the uptake of all sulfonate sulfur sources transported via the TauABC and SsuABC systems.
L231: A third group of mutants carried various combinations of deletions that abolished the function of a periplasmic component, an integral membrane component, and an ATP-binding protein of either transport system. Six out of the eight possible combinations of multiple deletion mutants were obtained (Fig. 【78†2】G to L), and the growth properties of these mutants were expected to provide information on the exchangeability of components between the TauABC and SsuABC transport systems.
L232: Attempts to obtain the multiple deletion ΔtauABC and ΔssuA ΔssuB ΔtauC strains by using the chromosomal mutagenesis system described by Link et al. (【69†10】) were unsuccessful, and their construction was not pursued further.

L236: In addition to mutants with components of the TauABC and SsuABC transport systems deleted, strains lacking either the SsuD or TauD desulfonation enzyme were constructed. These mutants served to correlate growth with a particular alkanesulfonate as a sulfur source with the presence of either one of these enzymes and to verify whether the range of alkanesulfonates utilized corresponded to the previously established substrate range of the purified enzymes (【58†3】, 【60†4】).
L237: An ssuD tauD double mutant was important for establishing the amount of background growth in growth experiments. Since this strain lacked both α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase and alkanesulfonate monooxygenase, growth of this mutant on medium containing a particular alkanesulfonate as the only sulfur source was considered to be due to nonsulfonate sulfur contaminants present in the alkanesulfonate preparation used.
L238: ### Growth of wild-type and deletion strains with alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources.
L239: Growth was tested in a medium containing one of the following sulfonates as the only sulfur source: taurine, isethionate (2-hydroxyethanesulfonic acid), 3-aminopropanesulfonate, HEPES, MOPS, PIPES, 2-(4-pyridyl)ethanesulfonate,N-phenyltaurine, 1,3-dioxo-2-isoindoline-ethanesulfonate, 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonate, sulfoacetate, ethanesulfonate, propanesulfonate, butanesulfonate, pentanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate, octanesulfonate, decanesulfonate, and dodecanesulfonate.
L240: All of these compounds have been shown to be substrates for the TauD and/or the SsuD enzyme (【58†3】, 【60†4】). The qualitative assessment of growth with each of the 19 sulfonates tested was based on a comparison of the growth characteristics of each mutant with growth of the wild type. The wild type defined the upper level of growth, while the ssuD tauD double mutant served as a reference for zero growth with a particular sulfonate sulfur source.
L241: Growth of the deletion mutants on different sulfur sources was graded as described in Table 【80†3】, footnotea. The growth curves of the ΔssuA and the ΔssuCB mutants shown in Fig.【81†3】 illustrate the four arbitrarily established growth categories. From Fig. 【81†3】 it is also evident that growth with sulfonate sulfur sources was diauxic, with a first, minor growth phase presumably supported by contaminating sulfate and a second, longer growth phase reflecting sulfonate utilization.
L242: Diauxic growth was not observed when strains were cultured with sulfate as a source of sulfur. Furthermore, mutants in which transporter genes were deleted grew faster than the wild-type strain on either sulfate or sulfonates as a sulfur source. However, depending on the sulfonate sulfur source tested, fluctuations in the growth rate and length of the lag phase were noted.
L243: Since strains lacking TauD or SsuD grew like the wild type, we presume that these phenomena have their origin at the level of the transport of alkanesulfonates.
L244: Fig. 3.
L245: 【82†Image】Fig. 3. Growth of E. coli EC1250 and deletion mutants. Cells were grown in a microtiter plate as described in Materials and Methods (150-μl cultures). The optical density at 600 nm (OD_{600 nm}) was recorded with a microtiter plate reader every 5 min over 24 h. Every fifth measurement is shown. Only the growth profiles obtained with mutants grown on 1,3-dioxo-2-isoindolineethanesulfonate (A), butanesulfonate (B), PIPES (C), and MOPS (D) are shown.
L246: The optical densities obtained ranged from 0.25 to 0.5 and corresponded to optical densities of 1.0 to 2.0 when measured with a 1-cm light path in a Uvikon P-810 spectrophotometer.
L247: ### Specificity of the TauABC and SsuABC transporters.
L248: Table【80†3】 summarizes the growth phenotypes of the different E. coli constructs that carried one or more deletions in the genes for the putative TauABC and SsuABC transporters. The growth data indicate that taurine entered the cell exclusively via the TauABC transporter, whereas N-phenyltaurine, 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonate, sulfoacetate, ethanesulfonate, propanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate, octanesulfonate, decanesulfonate, MOPS, and HEPES were transported only by the SsuABC transporter.
L249: Some sulfonates were taken up via both the TauABC and the SsuABC systems. These included PIPES, 2-(4-pyridyl)ethanesulfonate, isethionate, 1,3-dioxo-2-isoindolineethanesulfonate, 3-aminopropanesulfonate, butanesulfonate, and pentanesulfonate, 1,3-Dioxo-2-isoindolineethanesulfonate and 3-aminopropanesulfonate appeared to be transported with the same efficiency by both systems. Figure 【83†4】 summarizes these data.
L250: Comparison of this scheme with the previously reported substrate ranges of the TauD and SsuD desulfonation enzymes (【58†3】, 【60†4】) indicates that the range of substrates transported by the SsuABC system is congruent with the substrate specificity of its desulfonation enzyme. This rule does not apply to the TauABC system, whose desulfonation enzyme reacts with propanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate, and MOPS, compounds that enter the cell exclusively via the SsuABC transporter.

L284: As is evident from Table 【80†3】, propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate served as sulfur sources and enabled some growth of all deletion mutants examined. This suggests that these compounds enter the cell to some extent by a mechanism different from active transport by the SsuABC and TauABC systems.
L285: To test whether triple deletion mutants such as strains EC1250 ΔtauA ΔssuB ΔtauC, EC1250 ΔssuA ΔtauB ΔssuC, EC1250 ΔssuA ΔtauBC, and EC1250 ΔtauAΔssuCB are able to form functional hybrid transporters, these strains were inoculated into minimal medium containing one of the alkanesulfonates that are transported by both the SsuABC and the TauABC systems. The absence of growth under these conditions indicated that productive interaction between components of the two transport systems does not occur.
L286: ### Complementation analysis of deletion mutants.
L287: For the construction of complementation plasmids, it was assumed that chromosomal in-frame deletions would not affect the expression of the genes located upstream of the deleted gene or group of genes. Therefore, the genetic information available on the complementation plasmids started with the regulatory sequences of the operon of interest and ended with the sequence of the gene that had been deleted on the chromosome (Fig. 【68†1】).
L288: In the case of mutants with multiple deletions, the complementation of each deletion was investigated separately, if necessary in an intermediary deletion mutant.
L289: ssu deletion mutants carrying the appropriatessu complementation plasmid showed wild-type growth. However, tauA and tauB deletion mutants carrying the corresponding complementation plasmids pME4727 and pME4726 did not grow on taurine to the wild-type level. This effect was traced to the presence of the tauA gene or 540 bp of its proximal part on the high-copy-number plasmid pUC19 (data not shown).
L290: The reason for the severe growth inhibition exerted by these plasmids is not known, but complementation of tauA andtauB deletions with constructs based on the low-copy-number vector pET-24a(+) (pME4733, pME4734) was successful.
L291: To confirm that an in-frame deletion of tauA did not affect expression of tauD, α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase activity was measured as described previously (【58†3】) in cell extracts of E. coli EC1250 and EC1250 ΔtauA grown on butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Identical levels of TauD specific activity were obtained from both wild-type EC1250 and mutant cells lacking TauA. The tauAdeletion thus did not influence the expression of the downstream genes.
L292: Taken together, these results show that the chromosomally located in-frame deletions did not affect other gene functions and that the observed growth phenotypes were solely due to the deletion of the gene of interest.
L293: ## DISCUSSION
L294: The E. coli TauABCD and SsuEADCB systems for the assimilation of sulfur from taurine and other alkanesulfonates have previously been characterized at the level of the biochemistry of desulfonation (【58†3】, 【60†4】). Besides containing the structural genes directly involved in desulfonation, the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons are thought to encode components of ABC transporters for sulfonates (【57†21】, 【59†24】).
L295: Based on the results from growth experiments and on sequence data, we postulate that TauABC and SsuABC form two distinct ABC transporters for uptake of alkanesulfonates. Sequence comparisons indicate that ABC-type transport systems involved in microbial desulfonation are also present inBacillus subtilis (【86†23】) and Pseudomonas putida (【87†25】). Like in E. coli, these are encoded in the same transcription unit as the desulfonating enzyme. The deletion analysis of the E.
L296: coli taurine and alkanesulfonate transport systems presented here goes beyond amino acid sequence comparisons; it attempts to characterize these systems in terms of the substrate range and functional exchangeability of their components.
L297: Our results demonstrate that the TauABC and the SsuABC systems complement each other with respect to the range of substrates transported. The substrate ranges of TauD and SsuD were to a large extent reflected in the substrate range of the corresponding ABC transporter. The substrate range of the SsuABC transporter fit that of the SsuD alkanesulfonate monooxygenase.
L298: This correlation is not maintained for the TauABC transport system, which was unable to transport HEPES, MOPS, and propanesulfonate, although these compounds are substrates for the TauD enzyme (【58†3】). Thus, two systems for alkanesulfonate uptake and metabolism are available in E. coli, with TauABCD being specifically involved in uptake and desulfonation of taurine and SsuEADCB being an uptake and desulfonation system for a wide range of alkanesulfonates other than taurine.
L299: In the systems examined in this work, deletion strains that produced the substrate-binding protein of one transporter and the membrane component of the other did not grow with the sulfonates transported by either TauABC or SsuABC. Also, the formation of productive hybrid transporters in which the membrane component would be composed of the ATP-binding protein (SsuB or TauB) of one transporter and the membrane-spanning protein (SsuC or TauC) of the other transporter did not occur.
L300: The failure of hybrid transporters to support growth extended to alkanesulfonates that were common substrates of both wild-type transporters. It therefore appears to be due to the lack of interaction between the individual components of hybrid systems rather than to restrictions imposed by substrate specificity. An exception was noted when propanesulfonate or butanesulfonate was offered as a sulfur source.
L301: These compounds enabled growth, at respectable levels, of strains EC1250 ΔtauA ΔssuA and EC1250 ΔtauBC ΔssuCB as well as of mutants producing hybrid transporters (Table 【80†3】). In addition to being transported by the TauABC and/or the SsuABC system, propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate appear to enter the cell by an as-yet-unknown mechanism. Since both compounds are fully ionized under physiological conditions (【88†8】), their entrance into the cytoplasm by passive diffusion seems unlikely.
L302: There are few reports on functional exchangeability of the components of ABC transporters in the literature. ATP-binding proteins of ABC transporters have domains in common that were shown to be functionally interchangeable in the recombinant hybrid protein HisP-MalK ofSalmonella typhimurium. This protein was fully active in maltose transport but failed to complement a hisP deletion mutation (【89†17】).
L303: This observation indicated that HisP and MalK share domains that are exchangeable, whereas other domains confer system specificity by providing for interactions between the membrane-spanning protein and the ATP-binding protein (【90†12】, 【89†17】). Furthermore, complete ATP-binding proteins have successfully been exchanged between the Mal and Ugp transporters, which in E. coli transport maltose and sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, respectively (【91†5】).
L304: The N-terminal parts of the UgpC and MalK proteins exhibit approximately 60% sequence identity, which is much higher than the 35.6% sequence identity over the first 150 amino acids between the TauB and SsuB proteins.
L305: Periplasmic binding proteins for sulfonates and sulfate esters fromE. coli, B. subtilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and P. putida share between 22 and 45% sequence identity (【87†25】). They are less than 15% identical to other solute-binding proteins and form a family of binding proteins separate from those previously defined by Tam and Saier (【92†19】).
L306: TauA and SsuA are members of this family, but they exhibit only 22.7% sequence identity and were found to be unable to substitute for each other (Table 【80†3】). This is in contrast to theE. coli uptake systems for sulfate and thiosulfate (【93†18】) and lysine-arginine-ornithine and histidine (【94†13】), where two binding proteins of overlapping substrate specificity interact with a unique membrane component.
L307: The sulfate- and thiosulfate-binding proteins show 45% sequence identity, and the lysine-arginine-ornithine- and histidine-binding proteins are 70% identical.
L308: The proteins of the two postulated independent transport systems ofE. coli for taurine on the one hand and alkanesulfonates on the other exhibit low sequence identity but share a common physiological role. As documented by the mechanisms regulating gene expression in these systems, they both are involved in scavenging sulfur for growth.

L74: # Deletion Analysis of the Escherichia coli Taurine and Alkanesulfonate Transport Systems

L83: ## ABSTRACT
L84: The Escherichia coli tauABCD and ssuEADCBgene clusters are required for the utilization of taurine and alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources and are expressed only under conditions of sulfate or cysteine starvation. tauD andssuD encode an α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase and a reduced flavin mononucleotide-dependent alkanesulfonate monooxygenase, respectively. These enzymes are responsible for the desulfonation of taurine and alkanesulfonates.
L85: The amino acid sequences of SsuABC and TauABC exhibit similarity to those of components of the ATP-binding cassette transporter superfamily, suggesting that two uptake systems for alkanesulfonates are present inE. coli. Chromosomally located in-frame deletions of thetauABC and ssuABC genes were constructed inE. coli strain EC1250, and the growth properties of the mutants were studied to investigate the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources.
L86: Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants confirmed that the growth phenotypes obtained were the result of the in-frame deletions constructed. The range of substrates transported by these two uptake systems was largely reflected in the substrate specificities of the TauD and SsuD desulfonation systems. However, certain known substrates of TauD were transported exclusively by the SsuABC system.
L87: Mutants in which only formation of hybrid transporters was possible were unable to grow with sulfonates, indicating that the individual components of the two transport systems were not functionally exchangeable. The TauABCD and SsuEADCB systems involved in alkanesulfonate uptake and desulfonation thus are complementary to each other at the levels of both transport and desulfonation.
L88: In Escherichia coli, sulfate starvation causes increased synthesis of several proteins involved in scavenging sulfur from alternative sulfur sources (【56†15】). Recently, two sets of genes whose expression is derepressed in the absence of sulfate or cysteine were identified. ThetauABCD gene cluster, located at 8.5 min on the E. coli chromosome, encodes a sulfonate-sulfur utilization system that is specifically involved in the utilization of taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) as a source of sulfur.
L89: Disruption oftauB, tauC, or tauD resulted in the loss of the ability to utilize taurine as a source of sulfur but did not affect the utilization of a range of other aliphatic sulfonates (【57†21】). The TauD protein is an α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase (【58†3】), and the TauABC proteins exhibit similarity to ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transport systems (【57†21】). A second set of genes, the ssuEADCB gene cluster, located at 21.4 min on the chromosome, enables E.
L90: coli to utilize aliphatic sulfonates other than taurine as a source of sulfur. Deletion of ssuEADCB caused an inability to utilize alkanesulfonates but did not affect the utilization of taurine (【59†24】).
L91: SsuD is a monooxygenase that catalyzes the desulfonation of a wide range of sulfonated substrates other than taurine, including C_{2} to C_{10} unsubstituted linear alkanesulfonates, substituted ethanesulfonic acids and the buffer substances HEPES, MOPS (morpholinepropanesulfonic acid), and PIPES [piperazine-N,N′-bis(2-ethanesulfonic acid)]. This monooxygenase is dependent on reduced flavin mononucleotide (FMN) which is provided by the SsuE protein, an NAD(P)H:FMN oxidoreductase (【60†4】).
L92: The SsuABC proteins also appear to constitute an ABC transport system (【59†24】). Neither the TauD enzyme nor the two-component SsuD-SsuE monooxygenase desulfonated methanesulfonic acid, cysteic acid, or aromatic sulfonates (【60†4】), compounds that are unable to satisfy the sulfur requirement of E. coliEC1250. These two enzyme systems thus cover the full range of desulfonation activities in this E. coli strain.
L93: They convert alkanesulfonates to the corresponding aldehyde and sulfite, which has been shown to enter the sulfite reduction pathway to cysteine (【61†20】).
L94: In the present study we investigated the role of the tauABCand ssuABC genes in the utilization of taurine and alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources. The tauA andssuA genes encode putative signal sequences, indicating that their products probably function as periplasmic binding proteins. The sequences of TauB and SsuB and of TauC and SsuC are significantly similar to those of ATP-binding proteins and integral membrane components, respectively, of members of the ABC transporter superfamily (【62†6】).
L95: By analogy to known binding-protein-dependent ABC transporters (【63†2】), it is inferred that these systems are composed of a homodimeric membrane protein and a homodimeric ATP-binding protein. A pairwise comparison of the components of the TauABC and SsuABC transporters revealed sequence identities of 22.7% for TauA and SsuA, 40.4% for TauB and SsuB, and 34.5% for TauC and SsuC.
L96: Using a genetic approach, we explored to what extent the substrate specificity of the TauD and SsuD-SsuE desulfonation systems is reflected in the substrate range of the corresponding transport systems and whether components of the two transport systems are functionally exchangeable.
L97: ## MATERIALS AND METHODS
L98: 
L99: ### Chemicals.
L100: 
L101: All chemicals used as sulfur sources were of the highest quality available and were obtained from Fluka, exceptN-phenyltaurine and 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonate (Sigma), isethionic acid (Aldrich), and 3-aminopropanesulfonate (Acros Organics). Oligonucleotides were purchased from Microsynth (Balgach, Switzerland). Restriction endonucleases, T4 DNA ligase, andTaq DNA polymerase were obtained from MBI Fermentas.Pfu DNA polymerase was from Promega.
L102: ### E. coli strains and growth conditions.
L103: E. coli strain DH5α (【64†16】), used for cloning purposes, was grown with constant shaking (180 rpm) at 37 or 30°C in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium (【64†16】). Solid media were prepared by addition of 1.5% (wt/vol) agar. When appropriate, the following additions were made: ampicillin, 100 μg/ml; kanamycin, 50 μg/ml; chloramphenicol, 35 μg/ml; isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG), 0.5 mM; 5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl galactoside (X-Gal), 80 μg/ml; and sucrose, 5% (wt/vol).
L104: For plasmid isolation, restriction enzyme digestion, and transformation of E. coli, standard procedures were used (【65†1】). DNA for sequencing was prepared using either the QiaSpin Miniprep kit from Qiagen or the Jetstar Midiprep kit from Genomed.
L105: E. coli EC1250 (MC4100 trp-1) (【66†7】) and the corresponding deletion mutants of this strain were grown at 37°C in a sulfur-free M63 medium (【57†21】) supplemented with 4 μg of tryptophan per ml and the desired sulfur source at 250 μM. Growth curves were determined in microtiter plates with 150 μl of culture by using a SPECTRAmax Plus microtiter plate reader with SOFTmax PRO software (Molecular Devices).
L106: Overnight cultures grown in sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with sulfate as a sulfur source were diluted 100-fold in sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, and then 75-μl portions of the diluted overnight cultures were pipetted into the wells of a microtiter plate containing 75 μl of minimal medium supplemented with the appropriate sulfur source at a concentration of 500 μM. The optical density at 600 nm was measured every 5 min.
L107: The plate was shaken for 30 s before every measurement to ensure aerobic growth conditions.
L108: ### Construction of chromosomal in-frame deletion mutants.
L109: The DNA (at least 500 bp) flanking the gene or group of genes to be deleted was amplified using Pfu DNA polymerase. Oligonucleotide primers were designed to introduce adequate restriction sites for subsequent cloning purposes (Table 【67†1】). Their approximate locations in the tau and ssuoperons are shown in Fig. 【68†1】.
L110: Identical restriction sites were introduced at the 5′ end (around 20 bp downstream of the start codon) and at the 3′ end (30 to 40 bp before the stop codon) of the gene or group of genes to be deleted. The external primers used for PCR of the flanking regions introduced restriction sites available in plasmid pBluescript II KS (Stratagene). After digestion with the appropriate restriction enzymes, both PCR products were ligated together into pBluescript.
L111: The inserts of the resulting plasmids were sequenced to confirm that in-frame ligation had occurred and that no changes in the DNA sequence were introduced during PCR. Subsequently the deletion inserts were subcloned in plasmid pKO3 (【69†10】). All plasmids used for the construction of chromosomalE. coli EC1250 in-frame deletion mutations of tauand ssu genes are listed in Table【70†2】.

L213: In-frame deletion mutants of E. coli EC1250 were constructed as described by Link et al. (【69†10】) with some modifications.E. coli EC1250 was first transformed with a pKO3 derivative by using heat shock or electroporation (【65†1】). Transformants were selected at 30°C on LB plates containing chloramphenicol. On the second day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended in 0.5 ml of LB medium and diluted 10^{2}-, 10^{3}-, and 10^{4}-fold.
L214: A portion (300 to 500 μl) of each dilution was plated onto prewarmed LB-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 43°C overnight. On the third day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended and diluted as described above, plated on LB-sucrose plates, and incubated at 30°C overnight. On the fourth day, 100 to 500 colonies from the LB-sucrose plates were picked on LB-sucrose and LB-sucrose-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 30°C overnight.
L215: When possible, an additional screening on sulfur-free M63 minimal medium plates was done to find out which of the positive colonies (sucrose resistant and chloramphenicol sensitive) were unable to grow with taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source and thus were likely to carry the desired deletion. Putative deletion mutants were analyzed using colony PCR withTaq DNA polymerase.
L216: A single colony was resuspended into 20 μl of sterile deionized water, from which 1 μl was added to a 50-μl PCR mixture (【65†1】). The sequence of interest was amplified using the external primers used for the construction of the deletion; PCR products were analyzed on 0.8% TAE-agarose gels. Positive clones were purified on LB plates at least three times, checking each time for the presence of the desired in-frame deletion by colony PCR.
L217: For the construction of multiple EC1250 deletion mutants, a deletion mutant was subjected to another round of deletion as described above. Overall, the frequency of in-frame deletions obtained in successful experiments amounted to 1.4% of the putatively positive clones that were screened.
L218: ### Construction of tauD and ssuD tauDmutants.
L219: Since efforts to obtain an in-frame deletion oftauD remained unsuccessful, a tauD mutant ofE. coli EC1250 was constructed by P1 transduction (【77†11】). The tauD::lacZ fusion of the E. coli MC4100 derivative MW108 [Φ(tauD::lacZ)(λplacMu9)] (【57†21】) was transduced into E. coli EC1250.
L220: Kanamycin-resistant transductants were screened for inability to grow on M63 minimal medium with taurine as a sulfur source and for the formation of blue colonies on M63 minimal medium supplemented with glutathione as a sulfur source and X-Gal to confirm the presence of thelacZ fusion. To obtain an ssuD tauD double mutant, an EC1250 mutant with ssuD deleted was used as a recipient.
L221: ### Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants.
L222: Restriction sites which are unique within the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons were used to construct the plasmids shown in Fig. 【68†1】 and listed in Table 【70†2】. Plasmids for the complementation analysis of tau deletions were constructed in pUC19 (【75†26】), starting from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】). Plasmids required for the complementation analysis of ssudeletions were constructed in pBluescript II KS, starting with plasmid pME4221, which carries the entire ssu operon on a 5.6-kbEcoRI fragment (【59†24】).
L223: Growth of deletion mutants transformed with the appropriate plasmid was measured in 5 ml of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with taurine or butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Cultures were incubated at 37°C overnight, and the optical density at 600 nm was recorded on the following day.
L224: Alternatively, when growth of strains was investigated over a longer period of time, single colonies of the deletion mutant as well as of the strain transformed with the appropriate plasmid were resuspended in 50 μl of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, from which 20 μl was spotted on an M63 minimal medium plate containing taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source. Sulfur-limited solid media were prepared by the addition of 1.5 to 2% SeaPlaque agarose (FMC BioProducts).
L225: Two plasmids that contain the ssu and tauregulatory sequences located upstream of the ssu andtau operons were constructed (【57†21】, 【59†24】). A 340-bpBamHI-EcoRI fragment from plasmid pME4204 (【59†24】) containing the ssu regulatory elements was ligated into pUC19, leading to plasmid pME4822.
L226: For the construction of plasmid pME4821, which carries the tau regulatory sequences, a 450-bp BamHI-EcoRI fragment was PCR amplified from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】) using primers JP7 and JP8 (【57†21】) and finally subcloned into pUC19.
L227: ## RESULTS
L228: ### Construction of in-frame deletions in the tau andssu operons.
L229: Figure 【78†2】shows the functional transport components in deletion mutants that were constructed to probe for the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonate compounds. A first group of mutants lacked one of the putative periplasmic binding proteins (Fig.【78†2】A and B) or the membrane-associated components TauBC or SsuCB (Fig. 【78†2】D and E). A second group included constructs that were defective in the corresponding components of both transport systems at the same time.

L74: # Deletion Analysis of the Escherichia coli Taurine and Alkanesulfonate Transport Systems

L83: ## ABSTRACT
L84: The Escherichia coli tauABCD and ssuEADCBgene clusters are required for the utilization of taurine and alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources and are expressed only under conditions of sulfate or cysteine starvation. tauD andssuD encode an α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase and a reduced flavin mononucleotide-dependent alkanesulfonate monooxygenase, respectively. These enzymes are responsible for the desulfonation of taurine and alkanesulfonates.
L85: The amino acid sequences of SsuABC and TauABC exhibit similarity to those of components of the ATP-binding cassette transporter superfamily, suggesting that two uptake systems for alkanesulfonates are present inE. coli. Chromosomally located in-frame deletions of thetauABC and ssuABC genes were constructed inE. coli strain EC1250, and the growth properties of the mutants were studied to investigate the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources.
L86: Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants confirmed that the growth phenotypes obtained were the result of the in-frame deletions constructed. The range of substrates transported by these two uptake systems was largely reflected in the substrate specificities of the TauD and SsuD desulfonation systems. However, certain known substrates of TauD were transported exclusively by the SsuABC system.
L87: Mutants in which only formation of hybrid transporters was possible were unable to grow with sulfonates, indicating that the individual components of the two transport systems were not functionally exchangeable. The TauABCD and SsuEADCB systems involved in alkanesulfonate uptake and desulfonation thus are complementary to each other at the levels of both transport and desulfonation.
L88: In Escherichia coli, sulfate starvation causes increased synthesis of several proteins involved in scavenging sulfur from alternative sulfur sources (【56†15】). Recently, two sets of genes whose expression is derepressed in the absence of sulfate or cysteine were identified. ThetauABCD gene cluster, located at 8.5 min on the E. coli chromosome, encodes a sulfonate-sulfur utilization system that is specifically involved in the utilization of taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) as a source of sulfur.
L89: Disruption oftauB, tauC, or tauD resulted in the loss of the ability to utilize taurine as a source of sulfur but did not affect the utilization of a range of other aliphatic sulfonates (【57†21】). The TauD protein is an α-ketoglutarate-dependent taurine dioxygenase (【58†3】), and the TauABC proteins exhibit similarity to ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transport systems (【57†21】). A second set of genes, the ssuEADCB gene cluster, located at 21.4 min on the chromosome, enables E.
L90: coli to utilize aliphatic sulfonates other than taurine as a source of sulfur. Deletion of ssuEADCB caused an inability to utilize alkanesulfonates but did not affect the utilization of taurine (【59†24】).
L91: SsuD is a monooxygenase that catalyzes the desulfonation of a wide range of sulfonated substrates other than taurine, including C_{2} to C_{10} unsubstituted linear alkanesulfonates, substituted ethanesulfonic acids and the buffer substances HEPES, MOPS (morpholinepropanesulfonic acid), and PIPES [piperazine-N,N′-bis(2-ethanesulfonic acid)]. This monooxygenase is dependent on reduced flavin mononucleotide (FMN) which is provided by the SsuE protein, an NAD(P)H:FMN oxidoreductase (【60†4】).
L92: The SsuABC proteins also appear to constitute an ABC transport system (【59†24】). Neither the TauD enzyme nor the two-component SsuD-SsuE monooxygenase desulfonated methanesulfonic acid, cysteic acid, or aromatic sulfonates (【60†4】), compounds that are unable to satisfy the sulfur requirement of E. coliEC1250. These two enzyme systems thus cover the full range of desulfonation activities in this E. coli strain.
L93: They convert alkanesulfonates to the corresponding aldehyde and sulfite, which has been shown to enter the sulfite reduction pathway to cysteine (【61†20】).
L94: In the present study we investigated the role of the tauABCand ssuABC genes in the utilization of taurine and alkanesulfonates as sulfur sources. The tauA andssuA genes encode putative signal sequences, indicating that their products probably function as periplasmic binding proteins. The sequences of TauB and SsuB and of TauC and SsuC are significantly similar to those of ATP-binding proteins and integral membrane components, respectively, of members of the ABC transporter superfamily (【62†6】).
L95: By analogy to known binding-protein-dependent ABC transporters (【63†2】), it is inferred that these systems are composed of a homodimeric membrane protein and a homodimeric ATP-binding protein. A pairwise comparison of the components of the TauABC and SsuABC transporters revealed sequence identities of 22.7% for TauA and SsuA, 40.4% for TauB and SsuB, and 34.5% for TauC and SsuC.
L96: Using a genetic approach, we explored to what extent the substrate specificity of the TauD and SsuD-SsuE desulfonation systems is reflected in the substrate range of the corresponding transport systems and whether components of the two transport systems are functionally exchangeable.
L97: ## MATERIALS AND METHODS
L98: 
L99: ### Chemicals.
L100: 
L101: All chemicals used as sulfur sources were of the highest quality available and were obtained from Fluka, exceptN-phenyltaurine and 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonate (Sigma), isethionic acid (Aldrich), and 3-aminopropanesulfonate (Acros Organics). Oligonucleotides were purchased from Microsynth (Balgach, Switzerland). Restriction endonucleases, T4 DNA ligase, andTaq DNA polymerase were obtained from MBI Fermentas.Pfu DNA polymerase was from Promega.
L102: ### E. coli strains and growth conditions.
L103: E. coli strain DH5α (【64†16】), used for cloning purposes, was grown with constant shaking (180 rpm) at 37 or 30°C in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium (【64†16】). Solid media were prepared by addition of 1.5% (wt/vol) agar. When appropriate, the following additions were made: ampicillin, 100 μg/ml; kanamycin, 50 μg/ml; chloramphenicol, 35 μg/ml; isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG), 0.5 mM; 5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl galactoside (X-Gal), 80 μg/ml; and sucrose, 5% (wt/vol).
L104: For plasmid isolation, restriction enzyme digestion, and transformation of E. coli, standard procedures were used (【65†1】). DNA for sequencing was prepared using either the QiaSpin Miniprep kit from Qiagen or the Jetstar Midiprep kit from Genomed.
L105: E. coli EC1250 (MC4100 trp-1) (【66†7】) and the corresponding deletion mutants of this strain were grown at 37°C in a sulfur-free M63 medium (【57†21】) supplemented with 4 μg of tryptophan per ml and the desired sulfur source at 250 μM. Growth curves were determined in microtiter plates with 150 μl of culture by using a SPECTRAmax Plus microtiter plate reader with SOFTmax PRO software (Molecular Devices).
L106: Overnight cultures grown in sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with sulfate as a sulfur source were diluted 100-fold in sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, and then 75-μl portions of the diluted overnight cultures were pipetted into the wells of a microtiter plate containing 75 μl of minimal medium supplemented with the appropriate sulfur source at a concentration of 500 μM. The optical density at 600 nm was measured every 5 min.
L107: The plate was shaken for 30 s before every measurement to ensure aerobic growth conditions.
L108: ### Construction of chromosomal in-frame deletion mutants.
L109: The DNA (at least 500 bp) flanking the gene or group of genes to be deleted was amplified using Pfu DNA polymerase. Oligonucleotide primers were designed to introduce adequate restriction sites for subsequent cloning purposes (Table 【67†1】). Their approximate locations in the tau and ssuoperons are shown in Fig. 【68†1】.
L110: Identical restriction sites were introduced at the 5′ end (around 20 bp downstream of the start codon) and at the 3′ end (30 to 40 bp before the stop codon) of the gene or group of genes to be deleted. The external primers used for PCR of the flanking regions introduced restriction sites available in plasmid pBluescript II KS (Stratagene). After digestion with the appropriate restriction enzymes, both PCR products were ligated together into pBluescript.
L111: The inserts of the resulting plasmids were sequenced to confirm that in-frame ligation had occurred and that no changes in the DNA sequence were introduced during PCR. Subsequently the deletion inserts were subcloned in plasmid pKO3 (【69†10】). All plasmids used for the construction of chromosomalE. coli EC1250 in-frame deletion mutations of tauand ssu genes are listed in Table【70†2】.

L213: In-frame deletion mutants of E. coli EC1250 were constructed as described by Link et al. (【69†10】) with some modifications.E. coli EC1250 was first transformed with a pKO3 derivative by using heat shock or electroporation (【65†1】). Transformants were selected at 30°C on LB plates containing chloramphenicol. On the second day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended in 0.5 ml of LB medium and diluted 10^{2}-, 10^{3}-, and 10^{4}-fold.
L214: A portion (300 to 500 μl) of each dilution was plated onto prewarmed LB-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 43°C overnight. On the third day, five to seven chloramphenicol-resistant colonies were resuspended and diluted as described above, plated on LB-sucrose plates, and incubated at 30°C overnight. On the fourth day, 100 to 500 colonies from the LB-sucrose plates were picked on LB-sucrose and LB-sucrose-chloramphenicol plates and incubated at 30°C overnight.
L215: When possible, an additional screening on sulfur-free M63 minimal medium plates was done to find out which of the positive colonies (sucrose resistant and chloramphenicol sensitive) were unable to grow with taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source and thus were likely to carry the desired deletion. Putative deletion mutants were analyzed using colony PCR withTaq DNA polymerase.
L216: A single colony was resuspended into 20 μl of sterile deionized water, from which 1 μl was added to a 50-μl PCR mixture (【65†1】). The sequence of interest was amplified using the external primers used for the construction of the deletion; PCR products were analyzed on 0.8% TAE-agarose gels. Positive clones were purified on LB plates at least three times, checking each time for the presence of the desired in-frame deletion by colony PCR.
L217: For the construction of multiple EC1250 deletion mutants, a deletion mutant was subjected to another round of deletion as described above. Overall, the frequency of in-frame deletions obtained in successful experiments amounted to 1.4% of the putatively positive clones that were screened.
L218: ### Construction of tauD and ssuD tauDmutants.
L219: Since efforts to obtain an in-frame deletion oftauD remained unsuccessful, a tauD mutant ofE. coli EC1250 was constructed by P1 transduction (【77†11】). The tauD::lacZ fusion of the E. coli MC4100 derivative MW108 [Φ(tauD::lacZ)(λplacMu9)] (【57†21】) was transduced into E. coli EC1250.
L220: Kanamycin-resistant transductants were screened for inability to grow on M63 minimal medium with taurine as a sulfur source and for the formation of blue colonies on M63 minimal medium supplemented with glutathione as a sulfur source and X-Gal to confirm the presence of thelacZ fusion. To obtain an ssuD tauD double mutant, an EC1250 mutant with ssuD deleted was used as a recipient.
L221: ### Complementation analysis of in-frame deletion mutants.
L222: Restriction sites which are unique within the tauABCD andssuEADCB operons were used to construct the plasmids shown in Fig. 【68†1】 and listed in Table 【70†2】. Plasmids for the complementation analysis of tau deletions were constructed in pUC19 (【75†26】), starting from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】). Plasmids required for the complementation analysis of ssudeletions were constructed in pBluescript II KS, starting with plasmid pME4221, which carries the entire ssu operon on a 5.6-kbEcoRI fragment (【59†24】).
L223: Growth of deletion mutants transformed with the appropriate plasmid was measured in 5 ml of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium supplemented with taurine or butanesulfonate as a source of sulfur. Cultures were incubated at 37°C overnight, and the optical density at 600 nm was recorded on the following day.
L224: Alternatively, when growth of strains was investigated over a longer period of time, single colonies of the deletion mutant as well as of the strain transformed with the appropriate plasmid were resuspended in 50 μl of sulfur-free M63 minimal medium, from which 20 μl was spotted on an M63 minimal medium plate containing taurine or butanesulfonate as a sulfur source. Sulfur-limited solid media were prepared by the addition of 1.5 to 2% SeaPlaque agarose (FMC BioProducts).
L225: Two plasmids that contain the ssu and tauregulatory sequences located upstream of the ssu andtau operons were constructed (【57†21】, 【59†24】). A 340-bpBamHI-EcoRI fragment from plasmid pME4204 (【59†24】) containing the ssu regulatory elements was ligated into pUC19, leading to plasmid pME4822.
L226: For the construction of plasmid pME4821, which carries the tau regulatory sequences, a 450-bp BamHI-EcoRI fragment was PCR amplified from plasmid pUC18ALA4 (【76†14】) using primers JP7 and JP8 (【57†21】) and finally subcloned into pUC19.
L227: ## RESULTS
L228: ### Construction of in-frame deletions in the tau andssu operons.
L229: Figure 【78†2】shows the functional transport components in deletion mutants that were constructed to probe for the requirement for the TauABC and SsuABC proteins for growth on alkanesulfonate compounds. A first group of mutants lacked one of the putative periplasmic binding proteins (Fig.【78†2】A and B) or the membrane-associated components TauBC or SsuCB (Fig. 【78†2】D and E). A second group included constructs that were defective in the corresponding components of both transport systems at the same time.

# Audit of Eichhorn et al. 2000, Table 3

Neither file has real line numbers: each is one JSON string. I cite the embedded `L###` markers, which are shared between the two files. "Pub" is `publisher-web-extraction.json`, which covers L159–L308 and holds Table 3 and the Results. "Meth" is `publisher-methods-web-extraction.json`, which covers L0–L229 and holds the Methods. Its second fetch failed with a cache miss. Figures 2, 3 and 4 are images and are not retained. Nothing after L308 is retained. iML1515 lines refer to `benchmark/manifests/reference_data/ibex_extracted/gapseq_eval/gapseqEval/GeneEssentiality/models/curated/iML1515.xml`.

## 1. Table dimensions and genotype expansion

- **Size:** Table 3 has 13 genotype columns (Pub L256) and 19 rows (L258–276): sulfate plus 18 sulfonates. That is 247 cells, and none are blank.
- **Expansion:** the six deletable genes are tauA, tauB, tauC, ssuA, ssuB and ssuC. Each column expands to a 0/1 vector over those genes:

| Column | Genes deleted |
|---|---|
| None | wild type EC1250 |
| tauA | tauA |
| tauBC | tauB, tauC |
| ssuA | ssuA |
| ssuCB | ssuB, ssuC |
| ssuABC | ssuA, ssuB, ssuC |
| ssuA tauA | ssuA, tauA |
| ssuCB tauBC | ssuB, ssuC, tauB, tauC |
| ssuA tauBC | ssuA, tauB, tauC |
| ssuCB tauA | ssuB, ssuC, tauA |
| ssuAC tauB | ssuA, ssuC, tauB |
| ssuAB tauC | ssuA, ssuB, tauC (see the conflict below) |
| ssuB tauAC | ssuB, tauA, tauC |

- **Deletions are not whole genes.** They are in-frame, keeping about 20 bp after the start codon and 30–40 bp before the stop (Meth L110). They are not full ORF removals.
- **Genotype conflict, which must stay flagged.**
  - Pub L232 says ΔssuA ΔssuB ΔtauC could not be obtained and was "not pursued further". Table 3 still has an "ssuAB tauC" column.
  - Pub L231 claims six of the eight possible multi-deletion combinations were obtained, but Table 3 has only five triple-deletion columns.
  - Pub L285 lists only four triples, and none of them is ΔssuA ΔssuB ΔtauC.
  - Resolve this against Fig. 2 or the PDF before encoding that column. Until then, mark it `genotype_uncertain`.
- **Strains not in Table 3.** Single deletions of ssuB, ssuC, tauB and tauC, and the tauAB and tauABC deletions, appear in the plasmid list (Meth L184–195, L192–195). They are not in the table. ΔtauABC could not be made (Pub L232). The ΔtauD, ΔssuD and ΔssuD ΔtauD strains are described (Pub L236–237) but have no data in the table.

## 2. Ordinal categories

- **Scale:** −, <5%; +, 5–33%; ++, 33–66%; +++, >66% (Pub L279). The measure is net growth yield relative to the wild type, which is set to 100%. Each value comes from at least three independent experiments, but no per-experiment values or variance are retained.
- **Intervals:** treat these as intervals, not point values. The authors call them "arbitrarily established" (L241).
- **Wild-type column:** it defines the upper level of growth (L240, L279), so its all-+++ values are circular. Don't score them as measurements.
- **Sulfate row:** it is +++ in all 13 columns. Use it as a control row. Mutants even grew faster than the wild type on it (L242), so the top category saturates.
- **Non-monotonic cells.**
  - 3-aminopropanesulfonate gives ssuA ++ but ssuCB +++ and ssuABC +++. It also gives tauA ++ but tauBC +++.
  - Octane and decane drop in the tau deletions: octane is ++ in tauA and tauBC, and decane is + in both. The text still calls both SsuABC-only (L248).
  - Some of these are likely category-boundary noise. Score with ±1 category tolerance as the primary metric.

## 3. Missing observations (stated vs. tabulated)

- Pub L239–240 lists and counts 19 sulfonates, and Table 3 has 18. **Dodecanesulfonate is stated as tested but is absent from the table** (L271–276). Record it as `reported_tested_value_not_retained`, not as a negative and not as imputed.
- Methanesulfonate, cysteic acid and aromatic sulfonates (Meth L92) were not tested here. They come from the earlier Ref 60 and are out of scope.
- The tauD and ssuD single and double mutants (the zero-growth reference, L237, L240) have no retained data.
- Complementation results are "data not shown" (L289).

## 4. Strain, medium and normalization

- **Strain:** E. coli EC1250, which is MC4100 trp-1 (Meth L105).
- **Medium and conditions:**
  - Sulfur-free M63.
  - 4 µg/ml tryptophan.
  - Sulfur source at 250 µM final (500 µM was added to 75 µl, then mixed 1:1 with the culture; L105–106).
  - 37 °C, with 30 s of shaking before every read.
  - Microtiter plates with 150 µl cultures.
  - OD600 every 5 min for 24 h (Pub L245).
  - Precultures were grown on sulfate and diluted 100-fold.
- **Carbon source is not stated in either excerpt.** The M63 carbon source and the trace-element composition are missing.
- **Net growth is not defined.** The excerpts don't say which time point or what area was used.
  - Growth on sulfonates is diauxic. A minor first phase comes from contaminating sulfate and a longer second phase is sulfonate use (L241).
  - How the first phase is subtracted is not given.
- **Background:** the ssuD tauD double mutant is the stated zero reference, and its growth is attributed to non-sulfonate sulfur contaminants (L237, L240). Its values are not retained, so the "−" and "+" calls near threshold can't be audited.

## 5. Conclusions that must not become labels

- **Table 3 measures whole-pathway growth, not transport or enzyme activity.** Growth needs uptake, TauD or SsuD desulfonation, sulfite assimilation, and derepression under sulfur starvation (Pub L84). A "−" is never an enzyme-negative or transporter-negative label.
- **The authors' own data show the gap.** TauD desulfonates propanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate and MOPS in vitro, yet those compounds give no growth through TauABC (Pub L250, L298).
- **Don't derive TauD or SsuD substrate labels.**
  - Every one of the 19 compounds was pre-selected as a known TauD and/or SsuD substrate (L240), so the panel has no enzyme negatives.
  - The discriminating ΔtauD and ΔssuD data aren't retained.
  - L243 ("strains lacking TauD or SsuD grew like the wild type") is ambiguous, and it conflicts with the tauD screen for loss of growth on taurine (L220). Don't use it.
- **Don't encode "exclusively" or "only" transport claims** (L248).
  - Propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate allow some growth in all deletion mutants through an unknown entry route (L284, L301).
  - The octane and decane tau-deletion drops also contradict the "SsuABC only" call.
- **Don't label non-growth in hybrid strains as a mechanism for any other organism** (L285, L299–300). It is specific to these deletion constructs.
- **Polarity is only tested for ΔtauA.** TauD activity was measured in that mutant (L291). L292 generalizes to "did not affect other gene functions", which the retained text doesn't support. ssuA sits upstream of ssuD, so ΔssuA polarity isn't shown here. Complementation of tauA and tauB failed on pUC19 and worked on pET-24a (L289–290).
- **tauD was made by lacZ-fusion transduction, not in-frame deletion** (L219–220). Don't treat it as a clean deletion.

## 6. iML1515 leakage (checked in the repo copy)

- **Transport GPRs for 5 of the 18 table compounds already encode this paper's assignments.**
  - TAURabcpp is b0365 AND b0366 AND b0367 (tauA, tauB, tauC), at L106411–106417.
  - BUTSO3abcpp is (b0934 AND b0933 AND b0936) OR (b0366 AND b0365 AND b0367), at L114311–114324. That is the Ssu-or-Tau alternative shown in Table 3.
  - ISETACabcpp has both complexes (L118917–118924).
  - ETHSO3abcpp (L114352–114358) and SULFACabcpp (L116497–116499) have the ssu complex only.
  - MSO3abcpp (L119690–119692) is ssu only. Methanesulfonate is not in Table 3.
- **Other model reactions.** TAUDO is b0368. Five other reactions reference b0935 (L109116, 114119, 114240, 116266, 121138). I read the b-numbers from the model. The gene-name mapping (b0933 ssuB, b0934 ssuC, b0935 ssuD, b0936 ssuA, b0937 ssuE) is from my memory, not verified in the repo.
- **The other 13 compounds** (PIPES, MOPS, HEPES, 4-phenylbutanesulfonate, pyridylethanesulfonate, dioxoisoindoline-ethanesulfonate, 3-aminopropanesulfonate, propane-, pentane-, hexane-, octane- and decanesulfonate, N-phenyltaurine) had no matching reaction ID in my pattern search. That search was not exhaustive by metabolite.
- **Where iML1515 ships in the repo:** the file above and `benchmark/v3/results/nutrient-*/…/iML1515.xml.gz`. Any masked-function run on these models sees the answers.

## 7. FBA limitations for these measurements

- Table 3 is ordinal yield under sulfur limitation. FBA gives binary or continuous flux.
- iML1515 GPR logic would predict zero growth for the butanesulfonate double mutants (ssuCB tauBC). The table shows "+" in every deletion column (L270), so there is a built-in model/measurement disagreement.
- FBA has no regulation, so it misses derepression under sulfate or cysteine starvation (Pub L84). The sulfate-grown precultures also leave a contaminating-sulfate first growth phase that FBA doesn't have.
- The model is the MG1655 lineage, but the measured strain is MC4100 trp-1. A tryptophan supplement must be added to the in silico medium. The carbon source is unknown from these excerpts.

## 8. Concrete safeguards drawn from the sources

1. **Cell schema.** Store gene-level 0/1 vectors per column, the raw symbol, the interval bounds (0–5, 5–33, 33–66, >66), and a status. Statuses: `measured`; `control_by_definition` (WT column and sulfate row); `genotype_uncertain` (ssuAB tauC); `tested_not_retained` (dodecanesulfonate); `not_tested`.
2. **Label vocabulary.** Use only `growth_class(genotype, sulfur_source, medium)`. Add an explicit denial rule: no enzyme-function, EC, transporter-substrate or negative-substrate labels may be derived from the table.
3. **Medium record.** Record EC1250, sulfur-free M63, Trp 4 µg/ml, 250 µM sulfur, 37 °C, and carbon source = unresolved. Don't run FBA comparisons until the carbon source is obtained from the PDF or PMC.
4. **Scoring.** Score the 247 cells (or 234, excluding the WT column) in ordinal and ±1-tolerance form. Report separately the 3-aminopropanesulfonate, octane and decane cells, and propane and butane (growth in all deletions).
5. **Leakage stratification.** Before any masked run, strip the iML1515 GPRs for b0365–b0368, b0933–b0937 and the five linked reactions. Report scores split into the 5 model-covered compounds vs. the 13 others.
6. **Verification.** Cross-check Table 3, the Fig. 2 genotypes and the dodecanesulfonate row against the PDF and `pmc.html`/`bioc.xml` in the same directory. I did not read those here.

## 4. Strain, medium and normalization

- **Strain:** E. coli EC1250, which is MC4100 trp-1 (Meth L105).
- **Medium and conditions:**
  - Sulfur-free M63.
  - 4 µg/ml tryptophan.
  - Sulfur source at 250 µM final (500 µM was added to 75 µl, then mixed 1:1 with the culture; L105–106).
  - 37 °C, with 30 s of shaking before every read.
  - Microtiter plates with 150 µl cultures.
  - OD600 every 5 min for 24 h (Pub L245).
  - Precultures were grown on sulfate and diluted 100-fold.
- **Carbon source is not stated in either excerpt.** The M63 carbon source and the trace-element composition are missing.
- **Net growth is not defined.** The excerpts don't say which time point or what area was used.
  - Growth on sulfonates is diauxic. A minor first phase comes from contaminating sulfate and a longer second phase is sulfonate use (L241).
  - How the first phase is subtracted is not given.
- **Background:** the ssuD tauD double mutant is the stated zero reference, and its growth is attributed to non-sulfonate sulfur contaminants (L237, L240). Its values are not retained, so the "−" and "+" calls near threshold can't be audited.

## 5. Conclusions that must not become labels

- **Table 3 measures whole-pathway growth, not transport or enzyme activity.** Growth needs uptake, TauD or SsuD desulfonation, sulfite assimilation, and derepression under sulfur starvation (Pub L84). A "−" is never an enzyme-negative or transporter-negative label.
- **The authors' own data show the gap.** TauD desulfonates propanesulfonate, hexanesulfonate and MOPS in vitro, yet those compounds give no growth through TauABC (Pub L250, L298).
- **Don't derive TauD or SsuD substrate labels.**
  - Every one of the 19 compounds was pre-selected as a known TauD and/or SsuD substrate (L240), so the panel has no enzyme negatives.
  - The discriminating ΔtauD and ΔssuD data aren't retained.
  - L243 ("strains lacking TauD or SsuD grew like the wild type") is ambiguous, and it conflicts with the tauD screen for loss of growth on taurine (L220). Don't use it.
- **Don't encode "exclusively" or "only" transport claims** (L248).
  - Propanesulfonate and butanesulfonate allow some growth in all deletion mutants through an unknown entry route (L284, L301).
  - The octane and decane tau-deletion drops also contradict the "SsuABC only" call.
- **Don't label non-growth in hybrid strains as a mechanism for any other organism** (L285, L299–300). It is specific to these deletion constructs.
- **Polarity is only tested for ΔtauA.** TauD activity was measured in that mutant (L291). L292 generalizes to "did not affect other gene functions", which the retained text doesn't support. ssuA sits upstream of ssuD, so ΔssuA polarity isn't shown here. Complementation of tauA and tauB failed on pUC19 and worked on pET-24a (L289–290).
- **tauD was made by lacZ-fusion transduction, not in-frame deletion** (L219–220). Don't treat it as a clean deletion.

## 7. FBA limitations for these measurements

- Table 3 is ordinal yield under sulfur limitation. FBA gives binary or continuous flux.
- iML1515 GPR logic would predict zero growth for the butanesulfonate double mutants (ssuCB tauBC). The table shows "+" in every deletion column (L270), so there is a built-in model/measurement disagreement.
- FBA has no regulation, so it misses derepression under sulfate or cysteine starvation (Pub L84). The sulfate-grown precultures also leave a contaminating-sulfate first growth phase that FBA doesn't have.
- The model is the MG1655 lineage, but the measured strain is MC4100 trp-1. A tryptophan supplement must be added to the in silico medium. The carbon source is unknown from these excerpts.
